title: Last Pharaoh's Final Act
description: A smuggled entrance, a little heir, and a death no one can prove—five steps into Egypt's last active ruler.

questions.question: Smuggled past palace guards in 48 BC—Plutarch says in a bed-sack—which Ptolemaic queen was the first of her Greek line to speak Egyptian?
questions.explanation: The Ptolemies descended from one of Alexander's generals and had ruled Egypt in Greek for centuries. She lived closer in time to the iPhone than to the Great Pyramid's builders.

questions.question: That bed-sack delivery reached which Roman general—her first great alliance, years before Mark Antony?
questions.explanation: He was 52; she was about 21. Their alliance put her back on the throne and gave Rome a stake in Egypt's grain.

questions.question: She and that Roman general had a son, Ptolemy XV. History remembers him by what name?
questions.explanation: Alexandrians coined the nickname that stuck: "little Caesar." After her death, Octavian had the teenager killed. "Two Caesars," the saying went, "is one too many."

questions.question: Having sent Caesarion away for safety, how does legend say Cleopatra died in 30 BC?
questions.explanation: Even Plutarch admitted "the truth of the matter no one knows." Another rumor had poison hidden in a hollow comb.

questions.question: Cleopatra's legendary snake bite most likely came from which species—the same serpent that rears on pharaohs' crowns?
questions.explanation: Ancient writers said "asp." Historians who buy the story favor the cobra: its venom brings sleepiness without violent spasms—the dignified death Plutarch says she wanted.

imageHint: The golden uraeus crown worn by ancient Egyptian rulers, symbol of pharaonic power

easterEgg.title: Octavian's parade prop
easterEgg.text: Plutarch says even Caesar (Octavian) seemed to believe the asp story: in his triumph an image of Cleopatra was carried with the snake clinging to her. The body, he notes, showed no clear poison marks.
